title: Cell Types
intro: A cortical column is built from two families of neurons: excitatory glutamatergic cells (mostly pyramidal) that carry information within and out of the column, and inhibitory GABAergic interneurons that shape when and where that information flows. Three interneuron classes — PV, SST and VIP — cover most inhibitory cells and form a small set of repeating connectivity motifs that are worth copying into any serious column model.

blocks.text: Intuition: signal carriers and traffic controllers

Think of the excitatory cells as the vehicles that carry messages, and the interneurons as different kinds of traffic control. PV cells are fast traffic lights at the intersection right next to the cell body: they decide whether, and exactly when, a pyramidal cell fires. SST cells control the on-ramps far out on the dendrites: they decide which inputs, especially top-down ones arriving in L1, are allowed to count. VIP cells mostly control the SST cells: by switching SST cells off they open the dendritic on-ramps, a 'disinhibition' that lets context or attention boost a pyramidal cell's input.

items: Excitatory neurons: roughly 70–85% of cortical neurons, most of them pyramidal cells. Rodent estimates are usually near 80–85% excitatory; primate cortex has a somewhat larger inhibitory share.

Inhibitory interneurons: roughly 15–30%. In mouse, about 40% of interneurons express parvalbumin (PV), about 30% somatostatin (SST), and about 30% the serotonin receptor 5HT3aR, of which VIP cells are the largest subgroup (Rudy et al. 2011; Tremblay, Lee & Rudy 2016).

Dale's principle holds to a very good approximation: a neuron is either excitatory or inhibitory at all its output synapses. Sign-constrained weights are therefore biologically realistic, and the sign belongs to the presynaptic neuron, not the synapse.

blocks.text: Pyramidal neurons have a triangular cell body, several basal dendrites near the soma, one long apical dendrite running toward the pial surface and ending in a tuft (often in L1), and an axon that both branches locally and, in most cases, leaves the area. Their dendrites are covered in spines; a typical pyramidal neuron receives several thousand to a few tens of thousands of synapses (around 10,000 is a common round figure). Dendrites are not passive cables: NMDA spikes in thin basal and tuft branches (Schiller et al. 2000) and calcium spikes near the apical tuft (Larkum 2013) let one cell compute with many semi-independent subunits (Poirazi, Brannon & Mel 2003). This is the biological basis of the HTM neuron (see "The HTM Neuron" in section 4) and the subject of "Dendrites and Active Dendrites" in section 2.

items: Firing: regular spiking with spike-frequency adaptation for most cells; intrinsically bursting for many thick-tufted L5 cells.
Typical passive properties (in vitro, approximate): membrane time constant 10–30 ms, input resistance tens to a few hundred MΩ, resting potential near −65 to −75 mV.
In vivo rates are low and skewed: many cells fire below 1 Hz, a minority fire much more. Sparse, heavy-tailed activity is the norm.

Projection classes: intratelencephalic (IT; to cortex and striatum), extratelencephalic or pyramidal-tract (ET/PT; thick-tufted L5 to brainstem, spinal cord, thalamus), and corticothalamic (CT; L6 to thalamus). Harris & Shepherd (2015) argue these projection classes are more fundamental than layer labels.

blocks.text: In L4 of some primary sensory areas — rodent barrel cortex and primate V1 layer 4C among them — many excitatory cells are spiny stellates: star-shaped, spiny, without a prominent apical dendrite, and with axons that stay mostly within the local column, targeting L4 and L2/3. They are the main recipients of core thalamic input. Other species and areas use small 'star pyramids' in the same role. For modelling, they are local excitatory input cells with no long-range output.

items: Morphology: basket cells, which target the soma and proximal dendrites, and chandelier cells, which target the axon initial segment.
Physiology: fast-spiking, narrow spikes, little adaptation, short membrane time constant (around 5–10 ms); can fire at hundreds of Hz.

Connectivity: receive strong, depressing excitation from local pyramidal cells and from thalamus (so they are recruited quickly), and inhibit nearby pyramidal cells densely and with little selectivity, plus each other.

Function: feedforward inhibition that narrows the time window for integration to a few milliseconds, feedback inhibition that stabilises activity and controls gain, and generation of gamma oscillations (roughly 30–80 Hz). In models, PV cells are the natural home of fast E/I balance and k-winners-take-all style competition.
Morphology: the best-known type is the Martinotti cell, whose axon ascends to L1 and inhibits the apical tufts of pyramidal cells.
Physiology: often low-threshold spiking and adapting; excitatory synapses onto them from pyramidal cells are facilitating, so they respond more as presynaptic activity is sustained.
Connectivity: inhibit dendrites of pyramidal cells, and also inhibit PV and VIP cells, but rarely each other (Pfeffer et al. 2013).
Function: control of dendritic integration, including gating of top-down input and dendritic calcium spikes; surround suppression; slower, activity-dependent feedback inhibition.
Morphology: bipolar or bitufted, concentrated in L2/3, with vertically oriented axons.

Connectivity: their main target is SST cells (Pfeffer et al. 2013; Pi et al. 2013). They receive long-range input from other cortical areas (e.g. motor to sensory cortex; Lee et al. 2013) and neuromodulatory input (e.g. cholinergic).

Function: disinhibition. VIP → SST inhibition releases pyramidal dendrites from SST inhibition. Fu et al. (2014) showed this circuit raises visual responses in mouse V1 during locomotion. It is a candidate mechanism for attention- and context-dependent gain.

blocks.text: Other inhibitory types. Neurogliaform cells (often in L1, many marked by NDNF in mice) release GABA diffusely and produce slow GABA-B-mediated inhibition; double-bouquet cells have narrow vertical axons. Markram et al. (2004) catalogued the morphological and electrical diversity, and transcriptomic studies list dozens of types per area. For a column model the three-class PV/SST/VIP scheme is the usual and well-motivated compression.
Connectivity motifs (the math you actually need)

blocks.source:
Inhibitory motif, mouse V1 (after Pfeffer et al. 2013), arrows = inhibition

   PV  ──► Pyr (soma), PV            strong, dense, nonselective
   SST ──► Pyr (dendrite), PV, VIP   almost no SST → SST
   VIP ──► SST (main), few others    disinhibition: VIP ─┤ SST ─┤ Pyr

Excitation onto interneurons
   Pyr ──► PV   depressing, strong   (fast feedforward/feedback)
   Pyr ──► SST  facilitating         (recruited by sustained activity)
   long-range cortex, ACh ──► VIP     (context, behavioural state)

Order-of-magnitude local connection probabilities (within ~100–200 µm):
   E → E   ≈ 0.05–0.2      unitary EPSP ≈ 0.2–1 mV
   E → PV  ≈ 0.3–0.6       PV → E ≈ 0.3–0.6 (dense 'blanket' inhibition)
   Potjans–Diesmann 2014 uses within-L2/3 E→E ≈ 0.10, E→I ≈ 0.13,
   I→E ≈ 0.17, I→I ≈ 0.14.

blocks.text: The connection probabilities above are rough summaries of paired-recording and model data; they depend on distance, species, layer and age, and published values differ by a factor of two or more. What is robust is the pattern: excitatory–excitatory connections are sparse and individually weak, while PV interneurons connect densely to and from their neighbours. That pattern is why a few inhibitory cells can enforce sparse activity in many excitatory cells.

A balanced network in one sentence: each pyramidal cell receives large excitatory and inhibitory currents that nearly cancel, so it fires irregularly when fluctuations cross threshold (van Vreeswijk & Sompolinsky 1996; Brunel 2000). PV-like inhibition is what makes this balance fast enough to track input.
What this means for your model

items: Minimum viable: one excitatory and one fast inhibitory (PV-like) population per layer, roughly 4:1 E:I, obeying Dale's principle. This alone gives you stable, sparse, irregular activity and a k-WTA-like competition (see "Inhibition and k-Winners-Take-All" in section 3).

Make PV-like cells fast: shorter τm (about 5–10 ms vs 20 ms for E), no adaptation, strong and dense connections. In Diehl & Cook (2015) the inhibitory population plays exactly this role, one-to-one excited and all-but-one inhibiting.

Add SST when you have dendrites: if your excitatory neurons have an apical or contextual compartment (HTM distal segments, two-compartment models), SST-like inhibition onto that compartment is how you gate top-down or predictive input.
Add VIP when you have a context or attention signal: route it to VIP, have VIP inhibit SST, and you get multiplicative-looking gain on pyramidal responses without touching feedforward weights.
Use adaptation in excitatory cells (AdEx or Izhikevich regular-spiking parameters) and short-term plasticity on Pyr → PV (depressing) and Pyr → SST (facilitating) if timing matters.
Spiny stellates can be modelled as point neurons in L4 with local-only axons; pyramids benefit from at least two compartments if you care about feedback.
Don't over-split: dozens of transcriptomic types are real but unconstrained in a model. Start with E/PV/SST/VIP and add types only when a specific result needs them.
